papers.title: Uncovering mitochondrial diversity and candidate taxonomic lineages of Hypostomus (Siluriformes: Loricariidae) in Colombia
papers.abstract: Molecular data for Colombian Hypostomus remain sparse, limiting assessments of species boundaries. We combined two mitochondrial markers (cox1 and D-loop) with morphological, morphometric, geographic, and taxonomic evidence to evaluate diversity among Colombian populations. Using ASAP, bPTP, and GMYC, cox1 recovered 16-17 Molecular Operational Taxonomic Units (MOTUs), whereas D-loop yielded 32-37, indicating finer mitochondrial lineage partitioning in D-loop that was not consistently mirrored by phenotypic differentiation. Because both markers belong to the same non-independent mitochondrial linkage group, congruence reflects partition stability rather than independent multi-locus support. High taxonomic-assignment support was obtained for H. holostictus, H. hondae, H. niceforoi, H. plecostomoides, H. oculeus, and H. weberi, whereas H. carinatus, H. hemicochliodon, and H. sculpodon received moderate support and H. wilsoni remained provisional because voucher-linked verification of the sequenced individuals was unavailable. Seven candidate lineages remain unresolved (G1, G2, and M3-M7); M8 was not counted among them because the examined specimens were morphologically compatible with H. hemicochliodon. Among these candidates, Hypostomus sp. G1 and G2 showed method-dependent mitochondrial partitioning and differences in selected morphometric characters relative to examined topotypic H. robinii. G2 also differed in pigmentation from examined H. rhantos, despite morphometric overlap. However, morphometric classification performance in Magdalena specimens and unresolved diagnostic boundaries do not provide sufficient evidence for recognizing G1 and G2 as distinct species. Mitochondrial delimitation patterns can reveal lineage partitioning and help identify taxonomic priorities, but should not be equated with species boundaries. Broader sampling, verified vouchers, and independent nuclear or genomic data are needed to evaluate these taxonomic hypotheses.

papers.title: Allocating maternal-tree collections to conserve genetic diversity of Lumnitzera littorea in southern Vietnam
papers.abstract: Mangrove restoration nurseries often raise seed from a limited number of maternal trees, and how those trees are split among source populations affects which alleles reach the nursery. We genotyped 110 Lumnitzera littorea trees from two mainland and two island sites in southern Vietnam at 11 nuclear microsatellite loci and then enumerated all 5,236 ways of dividing a 30-tree collection among the four sites. With sample sizes matched, the mainland sites had consistently higher expected heterozygosity than the islands. Con Dao and Phu Quoc were the most differentiated pair on the full panel; dropping two influential loci put Can Gio and Phu Quoc at the top instead. Neither pattern changed when we compared the primary genotype calls with an earlier set of calls, restored 23 calls from overlapping adjacent peaks, or removed loci with high estimated null-allele frequencies. Taking 6, 8, 11, and 5 trees from Can Gio, Dong Nai, Con Dao, and Phu Quoc retained an expected 36.89 of 37 alleles on the full panel and 29.94 of 30 on the reduced panel. A nearly even split of 8, 7, 8, and 7 trees gave Phu Quoc better representation and cost little in pooled allele capture. Either split keeps all four provenances in a small collection; which one to use depends on whether a program values the site-private alleles at Con Dao more than balanced representation of every source.

papers.title: Limited biological identifiability of dominance-labelled variance components in polyploid genomic prediction
papers.abstract: Genomic prediction models for polyploid crops often partition genetic variance into additive and dominance-labelled components, but a fitted dominance component is not necessarily identifiable as digenic dominance (D2). We combined known-truth simulations with a panel-conditioned diagnostic workflow on 11 public datasets from alfalfa, potato, blueberry, guinea grass, rose, Miscanthus, sweetpotato and sugarcane. The workflow uses kernel geometry, permutation references, structure controls, planted-D2 spike-ins, posterior uncertainty and paired prediction tests. In autotetraploid simulations, the standard additive-plus-dominance model assigned appreciable variance to the dominance kernel when true D2 was absent, and its share responded only weakly to planted D2 signal. In crop panels, additive and dominance kernels were highly collinear, and Bayesian degree-kernel decompositions did not localize non-additive variance to D2, although restricted maximum likelihood placed it on D2 in alfalfa and potato. Observed shares exceeded matched permutation references by more than the pre-set margin in two of nine autotetraploid datasets, and no dataset met the criteria for biological D2 interpretation. A large fitted share was not sufficient for cross-validated prediction gain. We recommend reporting these components with diagnostics that separate biologically supported dominance, prediction-useful kernels and unresolved model-basis contributions.

papers.title: Population-scale measurement of human centromere array length variation from short-read sequencing
papers.abstract: Alpha-satellite higher-order repeat (HOR) arrays at human centromeres vary several-fold in length across individuals and have been linked to kinetochore function and chromosome missegregation. However, their repetitive megabase-scale architecture has largely restricted length measurement to a few hundred long-read derived genome assemblies, leaving short-read cohorts uncharacterized. Here we introduce cenlen, an alignment-free method that estimates active centromeric array lengths across all 24 human chromosomes directly from short-read or long-read CRAM files. To estimate array lengths, we first identify $k$-mers that are common within a query chromosome's centromere array but rare across other chromosomes. For acrocentric and other repeat-sharing families lacking private k-mers, cenlen instead models shared k-mer mixtures against assembled pangenome reference profiles using non-negative linear deconvolution. Across 61 genomes that were not used for training, cenlen estimates agreed closely with assembled array lengths (median relative error 2.4%), outperforming existing short-read estimators. We further optimized sequence retrieval and targeted k-mer counting, reducing CPU time 313-fold relative to existing methods. We applied cenlen to 2,557 individuals across genetic ancestries from the 1000 Genomes Project. Most variation in array length occurred within populations, but arrays on chr21, chr7 and chr16 differed between superpopulations more than the average common SNV. Finally, we found that array lengths were associated with molecular phenotypes, including splicing of MED14 in chromosome X. Overall, cenlen makes it possible to test associations between centromere array length variation and human traits in large sequencing cohorts.

papers.title: Reproductive fitness does not predict plastic changes in recombination due to diet in Drosophila melanogaster
papers.abstract: Meiotic recombination is a fundamental biological process that ensures proper chromosome segregation and generates novel genetic variation. Recombination rate exhibits plasticity in response to environmental conditions, yet how genetic background interacts with nutrition to influence this plasticity remains poorly understood. Using Drosophila melanogaster lines from the Drosophila Genetic Reference Panel (DGRP), we evaluated how varying caloric density affects X-chromosome recombination, body mass, fecundity, and survival across genotypes and over time. Caloric restriction significantly reduced female body mass in both genotypes, indicating a shared physiological response to dietary manipulation. Dietary treatment did not significantly affect egg-to-adult survival in marker-free crosses, whereas the high-calorie diet significantly reduced survival in marker-present crosses. After accounting for differential viability, we detected a significant genotype-by-environment (GE) interaction in X-chromosome recombination rates. Furthermore, shifts in recombination rate were not associated with reduced survival or fecundity, failing to support adaptive hypotheses as explanations for recombination plasticity. To assess overall ovarian gene expression during these dietary perturbations, we conducted ovarian transcriptomic profiling (RNA-seq) . Ovarian gene expression analysis revealed distinct, genotype-specific transcriptional responses to caloric restriction and excess calories, including significant changes in metabolic, stress-response, and cellular maintenance pathways across early and late time points. Overall, these findings demonstrate genotype-dependent recombination plasticity in response to dietary variation, without a consistent relationship between recombination rate and measured components of reproductive fitness, providing no support for the prediction of fitness-associated recombination under the dietary conditions examined. This work highlights the complex relationship of recombination rate plasticity among genotype, environment, and reproductive traits.

papers.title: Genetic Diversity and Geographic Structure of Nordic Rye Landraces and Historic Varieties: Expected Patterns and New Insights
papers.abstract: Rye has been an important food crop and source of nutrition in Finland for centuries and remains so today. Rye landraces and old varieties are still grown on farmers' fields. Interest in local landraces and conservation varieties has grown during the last decade due to climate change and its negative effects on biodiversity and resilience. We explored genetic diversity and population structure in Nordic rye landraces, historic population varieties and reference materials using complementary SSR and SNP datasets. For comparative analysis of genetic diversity, the Finnish varieties 'Riihi' and 'Reetta', the German inbred line Lo7, a German hybrid variety, the Estonian variety 'Elvi', and the landrace 'Sangaste' were included as reference materials. Both SSR and SNP analyses revealed geographically associated genetic differentiation within an otherwise largely shared Nordic rye gene pool. Notably, the independently sampled Mustialan and NordGen accessions of the Norwegian 'Tvengsberg' landrace were each clearly differentiated from the remaining rye material in the SSR and SNP datasets, respectively. Finnish landraces ('Aunus', 'Hermanni', 'Iivo', 'Joppe', 'Paakkola', and 'Taavetti') showed broadly similar genetic profiles, although substantial admixture was evident. In the SSR analysis, the Estonian accessions 'Sangaste' and 'Elvi' clustered together with 'Reetta', 'Riihi', and the Finnish landrace 'Polvijarvi', suggesting a closer genetic relationship among these accessions, although 'Polvijarvi' has previously been considered a distinct Finnish landrace. The Finnish variety 'Hankkijan Jussi' formed a separate cluster; this variety originates from a selection derived from the 60Co-irradiated Russian variety 'Vjatka'. The modern inbred line Lo7 and an unnamed hybrid variety were included as outgroup controls and showed clear genetic divergence from the Fennoscandian landrace material. Although Nordic rye landraces are often assumed to share a common ancestry and may have been influenced by historical seed exchange among farming communities, both SSR and SNP analyses revealed geographically associated genetic differentiation. These results indicate that regional genetic differentiation has been maintained despite the outcrossing nature of rye and the potential for historical gene flow.

papers.title: Contrasting microhaplotype diversity responses of saproxylic beetles to forest management
papers.abstract: Genetic responses to forest management may vary substantially among saproxylic beetles because species differ in habitat requirements, dispersal and ecological specialization. Here, we evaluated whether microhaplotypes reconstructed from Double Digest Restriction-site Associated DNA sequencing (ddRADseq) loci provide additional locus-level genetic information and reveal species-specific associations with forest protection, management and habitat characteristics across 12 saproxylic beetle species sampled in eight forest complexes in Poland. Phased combinations of linked Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNPs) within RAD loci were analysed as multi-allelic microhaplotypes. Observed microhaplotype diversity was compared with analytical expectations under linkage equilibrium to assess how diversity differed from that expected if constituent SNP positions were independent. Observed microhaplotype diversity was consistently lower than expected under linkage equilibrium across all 12 species, with the magnitude of the difference varying among species. Patterns of population differentiation inferred from SNP-based FST and microhaplotype-based {Phi}ST were significantly concordant in all species, although the strength of correspondence varied considerably among taxa. Individual microhaplotype homozygosity (FHAP) showed heterogeneous associations with site protection and management categories, with no consistent directional response across species. Sensitivity analyses restricted to the NE Poland detected no significant management associations after correction for multiple testing. Associations between site-level microhaplotype diversity and habitat characteristics also varied among species. Species traits showed suggestive associations with management-related changes in FHAP, although none remained statistically significant after correction for multiple-testing. Overall, microhaplotypes retain linked within-locus genetic variation and broadly recover SNP-based patterns of population differentiation, while associations between forest context and genetic variation remain strongly species-dependent.

papers.title: An isogenic platform to model the impact of sex chromosome and donor genotype in hiPSC-derived vascular smooth muscle cells
papers.abstract: Monosomy-X results in Turner Syndrome (TS), which beyond its cardinal height and reproductive phenotypes, spans incompletely penetrant cardiovascular phenotypes, including bicuspid valve, hypoplastic left-sided heart syndrome and aortic coarctation. These congenital heart defects (CHD) conspire with hypertension to dilate the ascending aorta, which can progress to rupture and drive early mortality in TS. Genetic contributors to incompletely penetrant phenotypes in TS remain only partially explored, thus complicating risk stratification. To begin addressing this challenge in donor-specific in-vitro models, we derived monosomy-X human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) alongside isogenic euploid control lines from donors mosaic for the second sex chromosome. In embryonic-origin specific vascular smooth muscle cells (vSMCs) derived from these hiPSCs, monosomy-X reveals donor-specific cellular and transcriptomic effects, with expression changes in one donor panel enriched in genes previously implicated in coronary artery disease and ascending aorta diameter. Polygenic risk scores (PGS) for cardiovascular traits mirror this transcriptomic enrichment, and suggest PGS analysis may help to prioritize hiPSC lines for in-vitro modeling of incompletely-penetrant traits related to TS-associated aortopathy.

papers.title: A switch in Nrg1-Rtg3 promoter recruitment coordinates mitochondrial cristae remodeling during the diauxic transition
papers.abstract: During the diauxic transition, Saccharomyces cerevisiae must preserve mitochondrial genome integrity while remodeling mitochondrial architecture for respiratory growth. The transcription factors Nrg1 and Rtg3 form a heteromeric regulator previously shown to be required for mitochondrial DNA maintenance, but its mitochondrial targets remained unknown. Here, we identify ILV5 and MGM101, which encode mitochondrial nucleoid proteins, as Nrg1-Rtg3 targets. Both factors occupied these promoters, with Rtg3 binding independently and recruiting Nrg1, providing a direct regulatory link to mitochondrial DNA maintenance. Unexpectedly, electron microscopy revealed that loss of either factor caused severe cristae defects even during fermentative growth, and these defects were more pronounced after the diauxic transition. Nrg1-Rtg3 also switched from repressing ATP20, ATP21, and MIC60 during fermentative growth to activating them after the transition. At the ATP20 promoter, recruitment dependence also reversed across the diauxic transition, from Nrg1-dependent recruitment of Rtg3 during fermentation to Rtg3-dependent recruitment of Nrg1 after the transition. Even as this dependence reversed, both factors remained necessary to establish the wild-type chromatin organization associated with each transcriptional state. Together, these findings show how one transcriptional complex can maintain activation of mitochondrial nucleoid genes while switching the regulation of cristae-organizing genes as cells transition to respiratory growth.

papers.title: isoGS: A genomic method to navigate the breeder's dilemma of diversity versus eliteness
papers.abstract: Global networks of public crop breeding programs exchange germplasm to share traits and increase diversity for genetic gain. There is a fundamental dilemma in crop breeding between the need to expand the genetic variation in elite gene pools while avoiding disruptions to essential traits required for eliteness. One particular challenge in admixed germplasm is the release of undesired transgressive segregation due to the disruption of favorable epistatic haplotypes of essential traits, which may stymie deployment of genomic selection (GS) In this study, we used breeding simulations to model recurrent population improvement for an annual crop species that can be selfed and crossed to examine the effectiveness of GS in admixed germplasm. We quantified the genetic heterogeneity between founder lines with an isoeliteness score, an effect size-weighted Hamming distance using quantitative trait loci markers. Populations with low founder isoeliteness (i.e. low genetic compatibility) had lower genetic gain with GS in early cycles than those with high founder isoeliteness (63% and 27% lower after 2 and 4 cycles). To mitigate this, we developed an isoeliteness-guided GS (isoGS) method to recover favorable epistatic haplotypes in a segregating population, which enabled 31% and 15% more genetic gain after 4 and 20 cycles. Our results suggest that founder isoeliteness scores and isoGS are valuable tools for overcoming the diversity vs. eliteness dilemma by managing the introduction of genetic diversity in a trait-specific manner.

papers.title: Lineage-specific LTR Retrotransposon Repertoires Engage OCT4-SOX2-SMARCA4 Chromatin Regulatory Architecture in Mouse and Human Pluripotent Stem Cells
papers.abstract: Long terminal repeat (LTR) retrotransposons contribute to regulatory sequences in mammalian genomes and provide binding sites for pluripotency-related transcription factors (TFs), such as POU5F1 (also called OCT4). SMARCA4 (also called BRG1), the ATPase catalytic subunit of BRG1/BRM-associated factor (BAF) chromatin-remodeling complexes, cooperates with pluripotency-related TFs and regulates chromatin accessibility. However, whether SMARCA4 preferentially occupies specific LTR subfamilies, whether it promotes chromatin accessibility at these elements, and how its occupancy relates to that of pluripotency-related TFs remains unclear. Here, we investigated the relationship between LTR retrotransposons and POU5F1-SOX2-SMARCA4 chromatin regulatory mechanisms in mouse and human pluripotent stem cells. Analysis of publicly available datasets revealed that SMARCA4 preferentially occupies specific LTR subfamilies, including RLTR13D6 and RLTR9E, in mouse embryonic stem cells. These LTRs exhibited accessible chromatin and active histone modifications, and were co-occupied by POU5F1 and SOX2. SMARCA4 depletion was associated with reduced chromatin accessibility and POU5F1/SOX2 occupancy at these LTRs, whereas POU5F1 depletion reduced both SMARCA4 occupancy and chromatin accessibility, suggesting cooperative binding. Taxonomic classification showed that most SMARCA4-bound LTRs belong to evolutionary young, rodent-specific families. Human pluripotent cells were also analyzed for the binding of POU5F1, SOX2, and SMARCA4, which revealed that a similar POU5F1-SOX2-SMARCA4 architecture engages primate-specific LTR families distinct from mouse LTRs. Our findings suggest that lineage-specific LTR repertoires can participate in a shared architecture of pluripotency TFs and chromatin remodeling factor. The association of evolutionarily distinct LTR repertoires with POU5F1/SOX2 and SMARCA4 in mouse and human pluripotent stem cells raises the possibility that non-orthologous, lineage-specific transposable elements were incorporated independently into similar regulatory architectures during mammalian evolution, generating lineage-specific cis-regulatory networks.

papers.title: Sequence-to-function embeddings across individuals capture rare and common variant heritability
papers.abstract: Statistical genetics learns how DNA shapes gene expression from variation across individuals, whereas sequence-to-function models learn from variation along the genome. Because sequence-to-function models map sequence to molecular readouts through deep architectures, their intermediate representations could offer function-informed descriptions of genetic variation. Whether these representations capture differences between individuals, however, is unknown. Here we introduce Embedding-based Heritability (EMBHER), a variance-component framework that estimates the expression heritability captured by these representations. Applied to Borzoi, embeddings recover much of the whole-blood heritability explained by genotypes and far exceed the model's final predictions. Deeper layers increasingly prioritize functional, evolutionarily constrained sequence while encoding less ancestry information than genotypes. Embeddings also explain more rare-variant heritability than genotypes, consistent with sharing information across variants too rare to estimate individually. EMBHER integrates sequence-to-function models with statistical genetics, a first step towards population-to-function models.

papers.title: Multi-resolution QTL mapping in four interconnected rice RIL populations reveals recurrent, background-specific, and environment-dependent loci
papers.abstract: We aimed to determine how marker density influences the detection and localization of quantitative trait loci (QTLs) in rice and to identify parental alleles with consistent effects across genetic backgrounds and environments. We evaluated grain yield, plant height, and flowering time in four interconnected recombinant inbred line populations at two Brazilian sites, Goianira and Boa Vista. Each parent contributed to two crosses, allowing us to compare the direction of its allelic effects in different genetic backgrounds. We compared a common backbone of 2,060 DArTseq SNPs with denser, cross-specific panels using marker and bin regression, interval mapping based on genotype probabilities inferred by hidden Markov models, and genome-wide permutation thresholds. The backbone recovered the major QTL regions. Peak positions differed by less than 100 kb in 14 of 19 comparisons within crosses and environments, including five exact matches. Across the four maps, densification increased marker counts 4.66-fold and recombination bin counts 2.44-fold. Recombination-breakpoint interval width decreased by 31.1% in Maninjau/Epagri 108 and 90.3% in Irat 122/Araguaia. Comparisons using the same lines resolved an apparent peak shift at qPH12 and placed qYLD2 below the genome-wide threshold in both panels. Four QTL regions recurred across crosses. Epagri 108 contributed all of them for reduced height at qPH1, whose interval contains SD1, and delayed flowering at qDTH8. Araguaia contributed an allele for earlier flowering at qDTH3 in both its crosses. The qDTH6 region recurred in Goianira, and the opposite flowering effects observed across environments in Irat 122/Araguaia mapped to different chromosome 6 peaks. Grain-yield QTLs showed less recurrence. The strongest associations, qYLD1 and qYLD6, occurred in separate indica/japonica crosses. In Goianira, qYLD6 explained 32.5% of phenotypic variance in the full-panel analysis and achieved genome-wide significance only at that site. Parental genome sequences helped prioritize candidate genes. Two complementary recombinants delimited a 247.0-kb region containing Ef-cd at qDTH3, while Hd1 and OsCLF remained genetically unresolved within a 51.8-kb marker-defined interval at qDTH6. These findings identify Epagri 108/Araguaia as a candidate cross for combining reduced height with earlier flowering. For grain yield, the favorable Maninjau allele at qYLD1 and Epagri 108 allele at qYLD6 warrant testing individually and together in recipient backgrounds under target growing conditions. Because the backbone was derived retrospectively, its economic benefit requires prospective evaluation. For routine marker-assisted selection, breeders could genotype founders and initial mapping families at high density, use a common panel of markers representing recombination bins to track validated haplotypes across subsequent families, and add cross-specific flanking markers to select progeny that retain a favorable allele within a smaller donor segment.

papers.title: Beyond Abundance: Integrated Splicing and Expression Quantitative Trait Loci Refine Causal Gene Mapping in IBD
papers.abstract: Splicing quantitative trait loci (sQTL) remain less explored than expression QTL (eQTL) in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). We mapped cis-eQTL and cis-sQTL in 1,149 colon samples from SPARC IBD participants in IBD Plexus, identifying 20,566 genes with eQTL (eGenes) and 9,906 with sQTL (sGenes). Colocalization prioritized 239 eGenes and 164 sGenes across 147 of 320 IBD risk loci, including 58 genes supported by both traits. We assessed candidate splicing consequences involving nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), 5' untranslated region remodeling, and protein domain alteration. In five genes with GWAS-colocalized eQTL and sQTL, risk alleles were associated with reciprocal changes in total gene expression and usage of junctions linked to predicted NMD-sensitive transcripts, consistent with NMD. IBD-associated sGenes were enriched in immune and inflammatory pathways and included drug targets. These findings motivate investigation of whether genotype-associated splicing differences, particularly those predicted to alter protein domains, contribute to variation in responses to IBD therapies.

papers.title: Reproductive competition amplifies purifying selection and reduces genetic load
papers.abstract: Deleterious mutations impose genetic load, and purging them through hard selection can carry substantial demographic costs. Competitive and sexual selection can instead remove deleterious variation through differential reproductive success. What remains unclear is when this process is more efficient than equivalent hard selection, and how competition generates this advantage. Here, we use forward-time simulations to express the impact of competition as an effective selection coefficient (se) calibrated against hard selection. Competition with multiple rivals strongly amplified purifying selection, whereas repeated contests improved discrimination by averaging stochastic and environmental variation. Strong competition also reduced genetic load relative to hard selection. These effects can shift weakly deleterious mutations from drift-dominated behaviour towards efficient purging. By front-loading purifying selection into reproduction, competitive selection can reduce genetic load at lower demographic cost. This provides a population-genetic mechanism by which genic capture can translate genome-wide genetic quality into more effective purifying selection. This may be particularly important in bottlenecked populations, where demographic recovery can relax purifying selection and allow genomic erosion to persist.

papers.title: First Broad-spectrum Sami and Norse diets in northern Norway over the last 4000 years revealed by sedaDNA
papers.abstract: The comprehensive specification of palaeo-diets has depended upon the preservation of plants and bones in archaeological deposits, which is limited by preservation conditions. Although middens at settlement sites in northern Norway can have comprehensive faunal archives they still may not reflect the full diet. Here, we apply sedaDNA metabarcoding and shotgun sequencing to two midden complexes in Finnmark, Norway. At both sites, this doubled the species identified. At the Bankgohppi "Gressbakken" house site (c.4.5-3.8 BP), items were added to all food categories (Figure below) including mammals such as reindeer, beaver, and bowhead whale, suggesting deep-sea fishing practice. At the Finnes coastal Sami Early Metal Age site (c.07-0.8 BP) and later Norse Medieval re-occupation, sedaDNA added terrestrial mammal (reindeer) and domesticated stock (goat, cattle) to the diet. The combination of traditional data with sedaDNA data provides us for the first time with a broad spectrum, suggesting seasonally balanced diets and fishing activity in northern Norway over the last 4000 years.

papers.title: Dual mRNA delivery corrects physical and biochemical deficits in a mouse model of hepatic onset trifunctional protein deficiency
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial trifunctional protein deficiency (TFP-D) is a rare, life threatening long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorder caused by variants in either the HADHA or HADHB subunits, leading to toxic metabolite accumulation and systemic energy deficiency. Current dietary management strategies are only partially effective and fail to prevent long term morbidity and mortality. Here, we developed a lipid nanoparticle (LNP) mediated mRNA replacement strategy to restore TFP function in a moderate severity TFP-D mouse model by delivering both Hadha and Hadhb mRNA. In cultured TFP-D mouse fibroblasts, dual mRNA delivery, but not single subunit replacement, rescued long-chain fatty acid oxidation and revealed a dominant negative effect exerted by the endogenous M404K variant Hadhb. In vivo, intravenous administration of dual mRNA-LNPs restored hepatic TFP expression, reduced circulating long-chain acylcarnitines, and improved physiological performance in aged TFP-D mice. Notably, intravenous delivery of dual mRNA LNPs significantly rescued cold tolerance test (CTT) performance by up to 71.6% compared to untreated and healthy controls. Together, these findings establish dual subunit LNP-mRNA delivery as a promising therapeutic strategy for TFP-D and support its potential applicability to other long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders.

papers.title: Structural correlates of disease-associated CTSC variants in Papillon-Lefevre syndrome
papers.abstract: Objective: To quantify structural features of disease-associated CTSC missense substitutions and evaluate a structural rule for research prioritization in Papillon-Lefevre syndrome. Design: We compared 16 ClinVar pathogenic or likely pathogenic missense substitutions with 234 recurrent gnomAD substitutions in the mature cathepsin C structure (PDB 1K3B). An expanded exploratory analysis included 35 further literature-indexed substitutions. We audited the documentation used to date the historical holdout and compared AlphaGenome splice scores with a consequence-only baseline. Results: Median predicted destabilization was 2.209 versus 0.763 kcal/mol (AUC 0.764, 95% CI 0.612-0.897). Catalytic proximity was observed in 4/16 versus 9/234. The expanded comparison gave AUC 0.740. Sixteen of 31 substitutions in the historical post-2015 subset had references dated through 2015. For noncoding variants, AlphaGenome splice scores and the consequence-only baseline both obtained AUC 1.000 on 12 positive and 105 negative ClinVar records. Conclusions: Predicted destabilization was associated with ClinVar label status in this dataset. The literature chronology and noncoding consequence composition limit claims of predictive validation.

papers.title: Minimal eukaryotic DNA polymerase zeta/Rev1 GC-pair mutasome
papers.abstract: In eukaryotes, translesion DNA synthesis (TLS) enables replication across DNA lesions, difficult DNA structures, and during replicative stress. While TLS prevents replication fork collapse, it is inherently mutagenic and requires tight regulation to prevent global mutation rates increase. Here, we show that elevated DNA polymerase pol {zeta}/Rev1 promotes spontaneous mutagenesis during replication. The five subunits of pol zeta complex (pol zeta5) are the catalytic subunit Rev3, the TLS polymerase Rev1, a dimer of accessory protein Rev7, the Pol31 and Pol32 subunits shared with replicative pol delta. Pol31 and Pol32 bind the Fe-S-containing C-terminal domain (CTD) of Rev3, which serves as a major assembly hub. We found that overproduction of pol zeta5, but not four-subunit pol zeta4 lacking Rev1 or Rev1 alone, increases spontaneous mutation rates by up to 20-fold, indicating that pol zeta5 can access undamaged DNA during replication and compete with replicative DNA polymerases. This mutator effect is independent of PCNA ubiquitylation. augments by hydroxyurea and synergizes with DNA mismatch repair defects. Overproduction of a pol zeta5 complex containing CTD-truncated Rev3 is also mutagenic, demonstrating that active TLS complexes can assemble and function without the canonical CTD interaction hub. Both complexes predominantly generate CG-to-GC transversions, a mutational pattern that resembles several COSMIC cancer mutational signatures. Inactivating Rev3 catalytic activity abolishes mutagenesis, whereas loss of Rev1 catalytic activity substantially reduces mutation rates and eliminates CG-to-GC transversions, identifying Rev1 as the primary cause of the observed mutation pattern. The findings reveal previously unrecognized mechanisms of pol zeta-dependent mutagenesis with broad implications for cellular evolution and cancer development

papers.title: Caenorhabditis elegans HLH-30/TFEB has age-dependent effects on the transcriptome and is required for normal progeny number and larval survival under basal growth conditions
papers.abstract: Background: The transcription factor TFEB/HLH-30 is a well-established regulator of autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis during starvation and stress, and it plays important roles in development and homeostasis. Our previous work demonstrated that Caenorhabditis elegans HLH-30 also functions under basal physiological conditions in mature neurons, where it promotes the expansion of endo-lysosomal degradative capacity during early adulthood. These findings raised the question of whether HLH-30 promotes lysosomal gene expression more broadly during early adulthood, and, more generally, whether its basal transcriptional functions depend on animal age. To address these questions, we analyzed the impact of hlh-30 loss on the transcriptome at two larval stages, L1 and L4, and two adult ages, Day 3 and Day 6, in hermaphrodites grown under basal conditions. Results: We identified modest effects of hlh-30 loss on the transcriptome that varied by stage/age. Enrichment analyses of genes downregulated in hlh-30 mutants identified functions related to defense response at L1 and in adulthood, and to cuticle development in adulthood. On the other hand, a role for hlh-30 in the basal expression of autophagy genes was exclusively detected in L1 larvae. A subset of genes encoding cathepsins showed decreased expression in the adult hlh-30 mutant; however, our results indicate that HLH-30 is not broadly required for basal expression of most lysosome biogenesis genes in adulthood. We also detected a trend toward reduced expression of genes involved in germline function at the L4 stage, when spermatogenesis occurs, and found that loss of hlh-30 resulted in reduced sperm and progeny numbers. In addition, we found that hlh-30 is required for full progeny survival through larval development. Finally, we identified a gene with increased expression at all four stages in the hlh-30 mutant, the germline transcription factor-encoding ztf-28. Knockdown of ztf-28 partially suppressed the reductions in progeny number and survival, suggesting that its increased expression contributes to these phenotypes. Conclusions: This study reveals roles for HLH-30 in transcriptome regulation under basal growth conditions that vary in both magnitude and content by animal age. Further, it demonstrates a previously unappreciated requirement for HLH-30 in promoting progeny number and survival, broadening our understanding of the physiological roles of this conserved transcription factor.

papers.title: A genetic toolkit of visible mutants for Caenorhabditis briggsae
papers.abstract: Caenorhabditis briggsae is a widely used model for comparative genetic studies involving C. elegans. Genetic analysis in C. briggsae depends on mutations with clear, easily recognizable phenotypes, yet most mutants reported so far have been mentioned only as names and linkage groups, without underlying experimental data. This study reports 183 C. briggsae mutants belonging to 11 phenotypic classes, which represent the most comprehensive collection to date. Almost all mutants were recovered in EMS screens of the reference strain AF16. Our analysis revealed that 121 mutations define 55 loci and 62 remain unassigned. A combination of complementation tests, linkage tests, two- and three-factor crosses, and polymorphism-based mappings helped place 51 loci and 15 further mutations to the six linkage groups. We report the supporting data, map distances, linkage groups, and corrections to several earlier assignments. Twenty-three loci correspond to molecularly identified orthologs of C. elegans genes, including six for which we report genetic, rescue, or sequence evidence here. The levamisole-resistant mutants fall into at least three complementation groups, two of which correspond to Cbr-unc-38 and Cbr-unc-29 (levamisole-sensitive nicotinic acetylcholine receptor a and non-a subunit, respectively). Transgene rescue experiments identify Cbr-dpy-1 (mucin-like), Cbr-sma-6 (TGFb type receptor kinase), and Cbr-unc-4 (homeodomain transcription factor), genes that have long been in use as genetic markers. In all cases, molecularly identified genes are located on the same chromosome as their C. elegans orthologs, although gene order within chromosomes differs. The strains, map, and underlying data provide a resource for genetic and comparative studies in Caenorhabditis nematodes.

papers.title: Intragenic redistribution of RNA polymerase II licenses epigenetic silencing
papers.abstract: Co-transcriptional chromatin regulation is widely recognized as a mechanism that reinforces active gene expression, yet transcriptionally active genes must also be able to transition into stable epigenetic silencing during developmental transitions and environmental responses. Whether and how ongoing transcription is coupled to the initiation of epigenetic silencing remains unclear. Here we show that elongating RNA polymerase II phosphorylated at Ser2 (RNAPII-Ser2P) functions as an instructive signal for epigenetic silencing initiation. At actively transcribed genes, RNAPII-Ser2P positions and spatially constrains the FLD-LD H3K4me1 demethylase complex near transcription termination regions, separating the complex from its gene-body H3K4me1 substrate. We found that both chemical perturbation of transcription and physiological silencing cues induce a redistribution of RNAPII-Ser2P into the gene body, accompanied by FLD relocalization and subsequent gene-body H3K4me1 erasure. FLD disengages from chromatin upon gene silencing, indicating that active transcription is required for its continued chromatin association. We further show that LD tethers FLD to RNAPII through an N-terminal HOX domain that binds the C-terminal region of FLD and an adjacent TFIIS domain that contacts the RNAPII CTD in a Ser2P-sensitive manner. This FLD-LD-RNAPII bridge is essential to promote H3K4me1 erasure and gene silencing. Together, these findings reveal a mechanism by which active transcription licenses the initiation of epigenetic silencing.

papers.title: Optimization of mitochondrial membrane potential contributes to extended longevity of daf-2 mutants in C. elegans
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial membrane potential is the charge difference across the inner mitochondrial membrane that is generated by the electron transport chain pumping protons from the mitochondrial matrix to the intermembrane space and is required for ATP synthesis, importing proteins into the mitochondria and movement of ions across the inner mitochondrial membrane. While a number of long-lived genetic mutants in C. elegans have been reported to have reduced mitochondrial membrane potential, increased mitochondrial membrane potential has also been associated with increased longevity. In this work, we examined the role of mitochondrial membrane potential in the long lifespan of daf-2 insulin/IGF-1 receptor mutants. We found that mitochondrial membrane potential exhibits a small but significant decrease in day 1 daf-2 mutants but a much greater decrease in day 8 daf-2 worms. We also examined the effect of genes and compounds that have been shown to alter mitochondrial membrane potential on daf-2 lifespan. Disruption of ucp-4, which increases mitochondrial membrane potential, decreased daf-2 lifespan without reducing wild-type longevity. Treatment with the mitochondrial uncoupling compound FCCP (carbonyl cyanide-p-trimethoxyphenylhydrazone), which decreases mitochondrial membrane potential, also decreased the longevity of daf-2 worms with no effect on wild-type lifespan. Combined, these results suggest that the altered mitochondrial membrane potential in daf-2 mutants contributes to their extended longevity and that their long lifespan is dependent on maintaining mitochondrial membrane potential within an optimum range.

papers.title: The genetic and environmental basis of hematopoietic chimerism in marmosets
papers.abstract: Common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus) have a high rate of twinning during pregnancy and exhibit an unusual phenomenon whereby stem cells migrate between fetuses in utero. These cells are integrated into a growing sibling resulting in each individual being a chimera of self and sibling. We mapped the distribution of chimerism across 145 marmosets by amplicon sequencing, showing high levels of chimerism in lateral mesoderm-derived tissues. By integrating pedigree and clinical records with estimates of chimerism we identified litter size to be a major determinant of chimerism and lifespan and demonstrate that chimerism and litter size are both heritable traits. Using exome sequencing of ~400 marmosets we identified major loci associated with variation in litter size and chimerism. These findings have implications for our understanding of self- and non-self across evolutionary biology, immunity and medicine.

papers.title: The genetic architecture of lipoprotein(a): simplicity, complexity, and mutability
papers.abstract: High levels of lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)) increase risk of cardiovascular diseases. Lp(a) concentration is primarily determined (>80%) by genetic variation at LPA, particularly by its large, size-polymorphic kringle IV-2 (KIV-2) repeat. However, because variation of the KIV-2 repeat is difficult to measure, the precise ways that genetic variants at LPA and other loci determine Lp(a) levels have been unclear, especially in individuals of non-European ancestry. Here, we developed new computational techniques to accurately genotype KIV-2 variation in whole-genome-sequenced population cohorts. Applying these methods to UK Biobank (n=490,414) and All of Us (n=245,394) provided insights into the genetic determinants of Lp(a) and the mutational dynamics of the KIV-2 repeat, which we found expands or contracts intra-allelically once every [~]500 generations. Variation in Lp(a) levels among people of all genetic ancestries was accurately predicted by a single, transferable genetic model capturing cis-epistatic effects of KIV-2 length and protein-altering polymorphisms in LPA. Controlling for predicted effects of LPA alleles revealed an additional, highly polygenic contribution to Lp(a) variation: LPA-adjusted Lp(a) levels associated with genetic variation at over 300 loci (P<5x10-8), much like other blood lipids. These results elucidate the genetic architecture and mutational origins of Lp(a) variation, showing how detailed characterization of a largely monogenic trait can provide surprising insights for complex trait genetics.

papers.title: Eukaryotic 45S ribosomal RNA spacers encode an ancient layer of antiviral response
papers.abstract: Eukaryotic 45S ribosomal RNA genes produce internal transcribed spacers (ITSs) that are excised and discarded during ribosome biogenesis, with no established function beyond rRNA processing. Here, we uncover an unexpected antiviral role for these seemingly expendable sequences. Comparative genomic analyses reveal extensive, evolutionarily widespread sequence similarities between eukaryotic ITSs and DNA viruses, particularly between vertebrate ITSs and herpesviruses. Across herpesvirus infections, ITS transcripts undergo striking, virus-specific remodeling, largely uncoupled from mature ribosomal RNA production. During herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) infection, hierarchical Bayesian comparison of competing dynamical models favors active host ITS deployment over passive viral remodeling by odds of 174,000:1. Experimental depletion of ITS2 consistently increases infectious HSV-1 production by approximately 70%, whereas supplementation with synthetic ITS2 RNA generally suppresses viral replication. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized antiviral activity within the 45S rRNA system, challenging the view of ITSs as disposable byproducts of ribosome biogenesis.

papers.title: Functional regeneration of the Rdl-A296S mutation in Anopheles funestus decouples insecticide resistance from genetic background and isolates its life-history costs
papers.abstract: Resolving the genetic basis of insecticide resistance in Anopheles funestus has been limited both by the historic difficulty of germline transformation in this species and by the confounding genetic and metabolic background present in field populations. The A296S resistance-to-dieldrin (Rdl) mutation provides an informative proof-of-principle case because it has persisted at high frequency in African vector populations long after the withdrawal of dieldrin. Here, we used a marker-less CRISPR/Cas9 homology-directed repair strategy to introduce the A296S mutation in isolation into the insecticide-susceptible FANG strain of An. funestus. WHO tube bioassays were used to quantify resistance across different dieldrin exposure regimes and to assess cross-resistance to other insecticides, while larval development and adult longevity assays were used to evaluate life-history effects. A296S alone was sufficient to confer strong dieldrin resistance. Resistance was context-dependent: homozygous resistance remained robust at higher exposures, whereas heterozygote protection declined with increasing toxic load. No operationally relevant cross-resistance was detected to DDT or pyrethroids. The mutation imposed a modest, recessive delay in larval development, with no detectable reduction in adult longevity and no clear net disadvantage across the life-history traits measured. This study provides the first in vivo functional validation of an insecticide resistance mutation in An. funestus. By isolating A296S on a defined susceptible background, it provides a quantitative baseline for the effect of a single target-site mutation and offers new insight into how stage-specific fitness effects may contribute to the long-term persistence of resistance alleles in natural populations.

papers.title: Continuous karyotypic and cryptic structural fluctuations drive acral melanoma evolution
papers.abstract: Reliable chromosome segregation during mitosis is essential for high-fidelity mammalian cell division. Even human cancers burdened by whole genome duplication and aneuploidy generally retain sufficiently stable segregation to produce clonal populations of progeny. Cancer genomes are accordingly understood to evolve in punctuated bursts, in which catastrophic rearrangement is followed by clonal expansion of a stabilized karyotype. However, bulk genomic sequencing, the workhorse of cancer genetics for the past two decades, cannot resolve structural variability within tumor subpopulations. Here we identify a subset of cancers that exhibit continuous ultra-low fidelity chromosomal segregation, with single tumors harboring individual cells whose metaphase chromosome counts ranged from 25 to over 200. This remarkable phenotype is recurrent in multiple cancer types and most common in acral melanoma, where it is associated with dicentric chromosomes, translocations, and complex structural variants. Single-cell whole genome sequencing revealed ongoing structural variation and the genomic signature of microhomology-mediated break-induced replication (MMBIR), a backup DNA repair pathway that triggers chromoanasynthesis. These genomes therefore do not pass through isolated catastrophic events and settle into stable lineages but rather undergo continuous evolution of chromosome number and structure across generations, resulting in extreme intratumoral heterogeneity and a shifting repertoire of gene fusions. We anticipate these findings will serve as a starting point for classifying tumors by ongoing karyotypic and structural fluctuation and for testing whether this state confers selective dependence on backup repair pathways.

papers.title: Site-Specific and Diet-Dependent Genetic Architecture of Trabecular Bone in Male BXD Recombinant Inbred Mice
papers.abstract: Vertebral fracture risk is influenced by trabecular bone (Tb) microarchitecture, a phenotype that is regulated by genetic and environmental factors. We examined the genetic architecture of Tb microarchitecture in the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) and its modification by dietary calcium (Ca). Male mice from 51 BXD recombinant inbred lines were fed adequate (0.5%) or low (0.25%) Ca diets from 4 to 12 weeks of age. Micro-computed tomography (CT) was used to assess seven L5 Tb phenotypes, and the response to Ca restriction (RCR) was calculated for each phenotype. Quantitative trait loci (QTL) were identified by composite interval mapping and compared with previously reported femoral Tb QTL from the same mice. Genetic background significantly influenced all L5 phenotypes and their responses to Ca restriction. We identified 127 QTL distributed across 61 loci. First, very few L5 QTL overlapped those previously identified in the femur, providing strong evidence for skeletal site-specific genetic regulation of Tb microarchitecture. Second, QTL detection was strongly dependent on dietary Ca, with only 4 of 33 loci identified under adequate Ca intake also detected under low Ca intake. Third, QTL controlling the RCR were largely distinct from those controlling L5 phenotypes under either dietary condition. Many loci affected multiple phenotypes, suggesting shared genetic regulation of Tb characteristics. Integration of genetic variation, expression QTL, and existing functional evidence identified plausible candidate genes at several high-priority loci. Together, these findings demonstrate that genetic regulation of Tb microarchitecture is both skeletal site-specific and diet-dependent, and that adaptation to dietary Ca restriction has a distinct genetic component.

papers.title: BPEA integrates pleiotropy and epistasis to guide allele pyramiding for multi-trait crop improvement
papers.abstract: Dissecting the genetic basis of complex traits and pyramiding favorable alleles are central to crop breeding. However, jointly evaluating pleiotropy and epistasis to identify allele combinations that meet multiple breeding objectives remains challenging. Here, we present BPEA (Bayesian Pleiotropy and Epistasis Analysis), a Bayesian framework integrating LD-guided QTL interval identification, joint genetic inference and allele-combination assessment. BPEA uses the joint posterior to estimate the posterior probability of simultaneous improvement (PPSI) between allele combinations and ranks them by mean PPSI. In simulations, BPEA improved interval identification and epistatic interaction attribution relative to comparator methods and maintained high precision in shared-signal detection. When epistasis was present, it reduced mean combination-selection regret by 68.4-86.3% relative to a model without interaction terms. Applications to three rapeseed populations identified shared genetic signals and candidate epistatic interactions associated with seed-quality traits. BPEA also prioritized allele combinations for simultaneous reductions in erucic acid and glucosinolate contents and identified complementary parents for cross design. BPEA thus provides a framework for genetic dissection and genomics-guided crop improvement.
